summary:
Himāchal Pradesh has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own in the available sources; a visitor to the state therefore operates under India's national framework, which Parliament altered on 25 March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting, with protests held in Mumbai on the day of passage. The amendment replaces the self-identification route established by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling and narrows legal recognition to the male and female categories together with historically accepted socio-cultural identities such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex people. Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The amended scheme conditions recognition and surgery on official process. Certification from a medical board and a district authority is required for gender-affirming surgery, and identity recognition rests on medical certification rather than self-declaration. The amendment also adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, amending the 2019 law. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor to Himāchal Pradesh, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment is contested terrain rather than settled policy. It was passed amid street protests in Mumbai, and the People's Union for Civil Liberties frames the new coercion offences as a revival of colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people, while the government frames the same measure as an expansion of welfare and anti-trafficking protection.

The direction of national legislation now runs against the direction of the superior courts. The 2014 Supreme Court ruling and the 2018 decriminalisation judgment broadened recognition and autonomy, and the Madras High Court issued detailed police and medical guidelines in 2021, whereas the 2024 criminal code change and the 2026 amendment narrowed safeguards and recognition.

Recognition coverage is a demographic question as well as a legal one. With an estimated two million transgender people in India, a scheme limited to traditional communities and intersex people removes a large and undefined share of that population from legal recognition, and the practical consequence is felt first where recognition is tested: documents, medical certification and identity checks.

Checkpoint risk is documented across several agencies rather than one, involving the Railway Protection Force, the Central Industrial Security Force at an international airport and passport authorities, which suggests friction is tied to the act of identity verification itself rather than to a single institution's practice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Himāchal Pradesh seeking legal recognition or gender-affirming surgery must now satisfy a medical board and district authority under the certification route introduced in March 2026; self-declaration no longer suffices under the amended scheme, pending presidential assent as reported.

People who self-identify as trans men, trans women, non-binary or gender-fluid outside the traditionally recognised socio-cultural groups are excluded from the recognition scheme and, on the government's own account, from the welfare schemes the amendment is said to widen.

The new coercion and alluring offences expose residents to prosecution with penalties of up to life imprisonment, a provision the People's Union for Civil Liberties identifies as echoing colonial-era criminalisation.

Since 2024, residents who experience sexual violence have lost the gender-identity-specific offences previously available under the Indian Penal Code, and community reporting indicates fear of increased assault under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Domestic remedy remains available. High courts have issued police sensitisation and anti-conversion-therapy directions in earlier litigation, and passport applicants have obtained relief against mandatory medical examinations, in February 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill has received presidential assent and been notified is unresolved in the available sources, which record it as approved by both houses and awaiting assent as of March 2026.

No Himāchal Pradesh-specific source is available on police handling of trans complainants, on the operation of the medical board and district certification route within the territory, or on any documented incident of violence against a trans person there; the national pattern is the only sourced basis for the assessment.

The local implementation record of the 2019 Act before the 2026 amendment, including any state-level welfare schemes, shelter facilities or sensitisation programmes for the Himāchal Pradesh Police, is not sourced.

How the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita has been applied to offences against trans people in Himāchal Pradesh since 2024 is not sourced; the national reporting on removed gender-identity-specific offences and community fear is the only available evidence.

The extent to which the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines have persuasive or binding effect outside the jurisdiction that issued them is not addressed by the sources.
